title: The domestic church (CCC 1655–1658)
hook: the family home as a little church

segments.voice: Yesterday, a covenant: marriage as a gift of persons, a partnership of the whole of life. Your line was covenant, not contract. Did you let the score go somewhere? Day one thousand one hundred eight.

Someone says grace, fast, before the food goes cold. It's a weeknight: homework at one end of the kitchen table, a laptop at the other, a pot on the stove. A toddler joins in late with the amen. On a shelf above the sink there's a small crucifix, a palm leaf from last spring gone brown, and a photo of a grandmother who died. It doesn't look like a holy room. The Catechism gives it a holy name all the same. That name is today's word.
screen: `GRACE, FAST, BEFORE IT GETS COLD.` → `A KITCHEN TABLE ON A WEEKNIGHT.` → `A CRUCIFIX ABOVE THE SINK.`

segments.voice: The Catechism starts in the Acts of the Apostles. More than once there, someone comes to believe in Christ together with their whole household. The jailer at Philippi, shaken by an earthquake, is baptized that same night with all his family. Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, is baptized with her household. These homes, the Catechism says, became islands of Christian life in a world that didn't yet believe. Then it reaches for a phrase from the Second Vatican Council: the family as the domestic church, the church of the home. Ecclesia domestica. Not a metaphor for something lesser. The home is where children first hear the faith, from their parents, by word and by example. It's where a vocation, any vocation, is first noticed. What happens there? The Catechism says the home is the first school of Christian life. There you learn endurance, and the joy of work, and love between brothers and sisters, and generous forgiveness, again and again. There the family prays together, and offers its life to God. So the ordinary things count: grace before meals, a blessing at bedtime, a fight made up before sleep. In Acts, Paul and Silas tell the jailer that if he believes in the Lord Jesus, he and his house will be saved. The promise is made to a household. And the Catechism doesn't forget people who live without a family nearby: the single, the widowed, people far from home. It says the Church's doors must be open to them, and that no one is without a family in this world: the Church is a home and family for everyone, especially those who labor and are burdened.
screen: `HOUSEHOLDS IN ACTS.` · `ECCLESIA DOMESTICA.` · `THE FIRST SCHOOL OF CHRISTIAN LIFE.` · `NO ONE WITHOUT A FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray at home with someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of who you share a home with: a partner, a child, a parent, a roommate, or no one right now. Picture one small moment today when the two of you could pause together: before a meal, at bedtime, on a phone call if you live apart. If you pray, you could say an Our Father together, or grace before eating. If you don't, a moment of quiet thanks at the table does the same work of noticing. Choose the moment now. The bell holds the time.
Domestic church. The home as a little church: the household where faith is first heard, prayed and practiced, with the Church's doors open to everyone without one. Today's word.
Your line: a little church. Today, keep the moment you chose, at a table, a bedside or on the phone, even if it's brief. Day one thousand one hundred eight.

howItsDone: Catholic families may say grace before meals, pray at bedtime with children, keep a crucifix or holy images at home, and mark feasts and seasons such as Advent and Lent around the table.
